title: Anomaly detection: spotting the odd one
hook: Thresholds, statistics, isolation, reconstruction and supervised models. Rare problems that keep changing.
inPlainWords: Anomaly detection learns what normal looks like and flags what does not fit. It is the tool when problems are rare and look different each time.

useCase.title: Spot suspicious orders and failing scanners
useCase.story: About 0.1% of ShopEase orders are fraudulent, and the tricks keep changing. Warehouse scanners also occasionally drift and misread labels. Few confirmed examples exist.

approaches.name: Fixed thresholds
approaches.what: Flag anything above or below a set limit.
approaches.avoidWhen: What counts as normal changes with the season and the customer.

approaches.name: Statistical comparison
approaches.what: Flag values far from the typical range for that customer or group.
approaches.greatWhen: One or two measures with stable patterns.
approaches.example: This customer normally spends $60. Today is $900.

approaches.name: Isolation-style methods
approaches.what: Randomly split the data. Oddballs get isolated in fewer splits.
approaches.greatWhen: Many columns, no labels, and you want speed.
approaches.avoidWhen: Anomalies that hide inside normal-looking clusters.
approaches.example: An order with an unusual mix of device, address and timing.

approaches.name: Reconstruction (autoencoder)
approaches.what: Learn to rebuild normal data. Bad rebuilds signal anomalies.
approaches.greatWhen: Complex data like sensor streams and images.
approaches.avoidWhen: Small data, where simpler methods work.

approaches.name: Supervised classification
approaches.what: Train on labeled fraud versus normal.
approaches.greatWhen: You have plenty of labeled examples of the problem.
approaches.avoidWhen: Labels are few, or new tricks appear that the model has never seen.
approaches.example: Known fraud patterns from past chargebacks.

approaches.name: Detectors plus human review
approaches.what: Combine detectors with a review queue and feedback.
approaches.example: Analysts confirm or dismiss alerts, and the results feed back.

challenge.question: Fraud is rare, keeps changing, and you have few confirmed examples. What is the best start?

options.text: An unsupervised detector plus rules, with a review queue that creates labels for later models
options.why: It catches new tricks now, and every review makes a future supervised model better.

options.text: A supervised model trained on the 40 confirmed cases
options.why: Too few and too old. It will only catch copies of past fraud.
Easy, but it misses small fraud and flags every big genuine order.

options.text: Ask a language model to eyeball each order
options.why: Slow, costly, and no better than the detectors.

bestCase.title: Layer detectors, and turn reviews into labels
bestCase.example: An isolation-style detector flags the strangest 0.5% of orders. Analysts review them and confirm about 1 in 6. After six months those confirmed cases train a supervised model for known tricks, while the unsupervised layer keeps catching new ones.

worstCase.title: One rigid rule, or a model trained on a handful of old cases
worstCase.example: A $2,000 threshold misses many small fraudulent orders and flags every big genuine order at Christmas. Or a model trained on 40 old cases catches copies of those and nothing new.

steps.label: Order arrives
steps.goes: A new order enters the system.

steps.label: Learn what normal looks like
steps.goes: The detector knows normal patterns for orders like this.

steps.label: Compare with a threshold
steps.goes: The score is above the review line.
steps.goesWrong: A fixed $2,000 limit lets this $940 fraudulent order pass.

steps.label: Analyst review
steps.goes: A person checks the flagged order.

steps.label: Feed back the result
steps.goes: Confirmed fraud becomes a label for later models.

takeaway: When problems are rare and keep changing, learn what normal is, flag the odd, and let reviews create labels.
